Patient demographics:
  age: 41
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 40

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Military Topics: Talks about military, Self-Consciousness: Being seen, Authority Figures: People in uniform
  Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control, Revenge Fantasies: I imagine getting revenge on the people responsible, People Pleasing: go along with whatever others want to feel safe
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger
  Negative Appraisals: Isolation: I feel isolated and set apart from others, Humiliation: I feel permanently humiliated by what happened, Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation

Vignette:
Rajesh was thirty-two when the men came to the compound. He had been working as a conservation volunteer in a remote region of the Philippines, part of a three-month assignment cataloguing endemic bird species in a protected forest area. The work had been demanding but purposeful—he was good at it, methodical, patient with the painstaking detail required to document migration patterns. On the third week, armed militants swept through the compound at dawn. They took four foreigners, including Rajesh. For nineteen days he was held in a makeshift camp, moved twice, kept in a concrete room with a single barred window. The room was small enough that he could touch both walls if he stretched his arms. They wanted money. They wanted statements. What they wanted shifted daily depending on who was guarding him and what news filtered in from outside. The uncertainty was its own kind of captivity—not knowing whether today would bring negotiation or punishment, whether the sounds of shouting outside meant rescue or execution. When he was finally released through a ransom payment and diplomatic intervention, he weighed fourteen pounds less than when he went in.

That was nine years ago. For the first six months after his release, Rajesh told himself he was fine, that he was lucky, that others had endured worse. He returned to the States, took a job with the National Park Service, and moved to a quiet region in the Pacific Northwest. He met Priya through a hiking group three years ago, and they had built a careful, quiet life together. But the careful life was increasingly a life of avoidance, and by the time Rajesh came to therapy at forty-one, the avoidance had become architecture.

At work, Rajesh had gradually shifted his patrol routes to avoid the ranger station where his supervisor, Captain Morrison, held his office hours. Morrison wore the campaign hat and uniform that came with the position, and something about the sight of him—the authority implicit in the fabric and insignia—sent Rajesh into a state of hypervigilance that made his shifts unbearable. He had taken to doing his paperwork at home, arriving before Morrison came in, leaving after he departed. His supervisor had begun to notice, had asked if everything was all right. Rajesh had said yes, of course, while internally calculating how to keep his job without having to see Morrison's face. When a documentary about military operations had aired on the news, Rajesh had felt his chest tighten at the opening credits. He had quietly asked Priya if they could watch something else, and when she had gently suggested that avoidance might not help, he had agreed with her immediately, apologized, and then felt a flash of resentment at her for making him feel foolish.

The flashbacks came without warning. A car backfiring near the trailhead sent him into a crouch, his body convinced for several seconds that the sound was gunfire. But it was the unexpected movements that sometimes undid him most completely. Last month, Priya had turned quickly from the kitchen counter to hand him a plate, and his entire body had seized—his hands flew up defensively, his breath caught, and for a moment he could not process that it was her, that he was safe, that a sudden motion was not a threat. She had frozen, the plate still extended, and they had both stood there while his nervous system caught up to reality. He would be walking through the forest—the work he loved—and suddenly he was back in the concrete room, the light through the barred window the same slant as the light coming through the trees, and his body would seize with the certainty that he was still there, that the nine years had not happened. These moments left him shaken, disoriented, and increasingly certain that his own mind could not be trusted. Even when Priya held his hand and told him he was safe, that they were in their home, he could not believe her. His body knew something she didn't.

For the past two years, Rajesh had restricted his eating to a rigid schedule and strict portions. It was the one thing he could control absolutely—what went in, when, how much. Everything else felt permeable, vulnerable to invasion. He had lost weight again, not dramatically, but enough that Priya had asked him to see a doctor. He had, and the doctor found nothing wrong. What the doctor could not measure was the small, hard satisfaction Rajesh felt when he closed the refrigerator without eating the extra portion, when his hunger became proof that he still had dominion over something. He had also begun to fantasize about the men who held him. Not constantly, but in the quiet moments before sleep, he would construct scenarios in which he found them, in which they experienced a fraction of what he had experienced, in which his powerlessness was reversed into absolute control. These fantasies were vivid and satisfying in a way that troubled him—he was not a violent man, or so he had always believed.

What finally brought Rajesh to therapy was a moment at work that felt like a reckoning. A new ranger, fresh out of training, had mentioned casually that his brother was in the Army, that he was proud of the military service in his family. Rajesh had felt something crack open in his chest. He had nodded and smiled and said the right things, but afterward he had sat in his truck for an hour, unable to move, thinking that he was forever separated from normal human conversation, that he would never be able to hear about the military without feeling like a coward, like someone who had failed a test of courage that others passed without even knowing it was being administered. He had called Priya that night and told her he needed help, that something was broken and he didn't know how to fix it. What frightened him most was not the flashbacks themselves, but the possibility that they would never stop, that at forty-one he would spend the rest of his life flinching at sudden movements, avoiding his own supervisor, unable to watch the news without his chest tightening. What he hoped for, though he barely dared to articulate it, was that he might someday trust his body again, that he might walk through the forest without waiting for the concrete room to swallow him whole.
